persists, however, not only in popular usage, but also in many other specifications from W3C and elsewhere.

Following publication of the Namespaces recommendation, there was\\n an intensive debate about how a relative URI should be handled, with \\nsome intensely arguing that it should simply be treated as a character \\nstring, and others arguing with conviction that it should be turned into\\n an absolute URI by resolving it against the base URI of the document.
The result of the debate was a ruling from W3C that relative URIs were deprecated.

Namespaces in APIs and XML object models
Edit section: Namespaces in APIs and XML object models
Different specifications have taken different approaches on how namespace information is presented to applications.

Nearly all programming models allow the name of an element or \\nattribute node to be retrieved as a three-part name: the local name, the\\n namespace prefix, and the namespace URI. Applications should avoid \\nattaching any significance to the choice of prefix, but the information \\nis provided because it can be helpful to human readers. Names are \\nconsidered equal if the namespace URI and local name match.

In addition, most models provide some way of determining which \\nnamespaces have been declared for a given element. This information is \\nneeded because some XML vocabularies allow qualified names (containing \\nnamespace prefixes) to appear in the content of elements or attributes, \\nas well as in their names.
